headline: State desk: New Hampshire files 7 cannabis requests; Alaska hours
dek: New Hampshire lawmakers filed two legalization requests and five medical ones; Alaska weighed ending its 5 a.m.-8 a.m. store closure.
key_points: New Hampshire legislators filed seven cannabis drafting requests for 2027 before the 18 November deadline, two of which would legalize adult-use sales.
One legalization request comes from a Republican, Rep. W. Packy Campbell, and would steer revenue to education funding and property-tax relief.
Alaska's Marijuana Control Board had a draft before it on 18-19 November that would repeal the statewide ban on retail sales between 5 a.m. and 8 a.m.
The Alaska draft would also let under-21s enter stores with a parent or guardian, without buying; no decision had been published by 21 November.
body: Two states moved on cannabis rules this week in very different directions. In New Hampshire, the only New England state without legal adult-use cannabis, lawmakers filed seven cannabis proposals for the 2027 session, including two that would legalize and regulate sales. In Alaska, one of the oldest adult-use markets, regulators looked at removing the statewide limit on store hours altogether.

Both items come from The Marijuana Herald's reporting on 21 November. The official New Hampshire bill-request database and Alaska's regulator website both refused our automated requests, so the details below rest on the Herald's account and our own earlier coverage; we flag where they could not be checked against the primary record.

New Hampshire lawmakers had until 18 November to file legislative service requests, the placeholders that become bills once drafted. Seven concern cannabis, according to the Herald. Full texts have not been published, so each is known only by a one-line description.

The first legalization request, LSR 2027-0669, comes from Rep. W. Packy Campbell, a Republican. It would legalize and regulate cannabis sales and use the revenue to support education funding and lower the statewide education property tax. The second, LSR 2027-0759, comes from Rep.-elect Kristopher Levesque, a Democrat, and would set up a state-supervised franchise model.

A Republican author matters in New Hampshire because of the veto math. As we reported on 8 November, Democrats are projected to hold 292 of 400 House seats and 15 of 24 Senate seats after the 3 November election, and Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte, who was re-elected, still opposes legalization. Overriding a veto takes two-thirds of each chamber, which in a full 24-member Senate means at least one Republican vote. Earlier this year the House passed a legalization bill, and the then Republican-led Senate voted 15-9 in March to table it, the Herald notes.

In our 8 November report, Rep. Jared Sullivan, sponsor of this year's House-passed bill, said he was drafting a new legalization bill. His name does not appear on the Herald's list of seven requests; we could not check the official database to see whether his proposal was filed under another sponsor or will come later.

The other five requests would change the Therapeutic Cannabis Program, which has run since 2013. Rep. Wendy Thomas, a Democrat, filed three: LSR 2027-0461 would let qualifying patients and their caregivers grow cannabis; LSR 2027-0543 deals with patients' use in hospitals, nursing homes and long-term care; and LSR 2027-0771 deals with how the program is run. Sen. Regina Birdsell, a Republican, filed LSR 2027-0663 on qualifying conditions, and Rep. Anita Burroughs, a Democrat, filed LSR 2027-0724 on possession and purchase limits.

Our New Hampshire hub records that, since October 2024, adult patients can be certified for any debilitating or terminal condition, and may hold 2 ounces and buy up to 2 ounces every 10 days from seven nonprofit dispensary locations. Home cultivation is the most significant change on the list: it would give patients a supply outside that small network.
> In New Hampshire the numbers to watch are not the bills but the senators: legalization needs one Republican to survive a veto.

Alaska's Marijuana Control Board met on 18 and 19 November with a draft regulation in its papers that would repeal the rule barring retail stores from doing business or admitting customers between 5 a.m. and 8 a.m. The draft would not replace it with any statewide hours, so stores could in principle open around the clock, according to the Herald.

Local rules would still apply. Anchorage, for example, requires stores to close between midnight and 8 a.m., so its shops would gain nothing unless the city changes its own rules. The same draft would allow people under 21 into stores when accompanied and supervised by a parent or legal guardian; they still could not buy cannabis or enter restricted areas or consumption lounges.

The draft was prepared under Gov. Mike Dunleavy's Administrative Order 360, a programme to cut regulatory burdens. The board's options were to send it to the Department of Law for review ahead of public comment, amend it, or return it to staff. As of 21 November the board had not published a decision, the Herald said.

The same meeting also had drafts that would double Alaska's daily concentrate purchase limit from 7 to 14 grams, as we reported on 16 November. Together, the drafts would make Alaska one of the more permissive retail regimes in the country on hours and purchase limits.

In New Hampshire, the drafted bill texts and their hearing dates are the next markers, along with whether any Republican senator signs on. In Alaska, watch for the board's published minutes from 18-19 November, and, if the hours draft goes forward, the Department of Law review and a public comment period before anything takes effect.
